query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under sustained loading, the progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers is primarily governed by the strain‐induced formation of localized amorphous bands at the nanoscale interfaces. These amorphous regions serve as built‐in stress mediators that gradually redistribute stress and delay abrupt dislocation glide, thereby enabling a balance between high strength and deformation tolerance.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating made of chemically complex high-entropy alloys that exhibit both FCC and BCC phases, with inherent severe lattice distortion and evidence of local chemical short-range order.
generation.intervention: Apply a sustained, creep-like loading protocol (strain-training) to the multilayer coating while preserving the nanoscale layered architecture.
generation.conditions: The test is conducted under a controlled, constant-load (or stress-controlled) regime at the service-relevant temperature (e.g., room temperature or slightly elevated) where the multilayer structure remains intact, and the loading is uniaxial to ensure a defined stress gradient across the multilayer interfaces.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized amorphous bands that form preferentially at the multilayer interfaces (and possibly near grain boundaries) as a result of concentrated strain and defect reorganization.
generation.mechanism: Because the severe lattice distortion and existing short-range chemical order in high-entropy alloys impede long-range, conventional dislocation glide, sustained loading concentrates stress in the interfacial regions. When a critical local stress threshold is reached, dislocation interactions and stacking fault reorganizations trigger an amorphous transformation. The emergent amorphous bands then act as a gradient mediator for plastic flow, progressively accommodating strain without inducing catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline behavior in which deformation is dominated by conventional dislocation slip with abrupt stress drops, the strain-trained multilayer will exhibit a gradual increase in the fraction of amorphous regions along the interfaces. This will be observed as a smoother, more homogeneous plastic flow (i.e., a reduction in stress serrations) and an overall moderated creep rate.
generation.baseline: A similar high-entropy alloy multilayer coating that, under conventional (non-strain-trained) loading conditions, deforms predominantly by dislocation-mediated mechanisms without significant amorphization.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable provided the multilayer architecture (with nanoscale layer thicknesses) is maintained and testing conditions do not induce complete loss of crystalline order (i.e., avoiding global failure or catastrophic shear banding).
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies in similar systems demonstrate strain-induced amorphization in deformation‐tolerant alloys, the exact kinetics and spatial distribution of these amorphous regions under sustained loading in a multilayer format remain to be precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a sustained loading (creep) test on the high-entropy alloy multilayer coating while periodically quenching the test specimens for microstructural characterization. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and diffraction mapping to track the evolution and spatial distribution of amorphous bands at the layer interfaces along with concurrent stress–strain measurements.
measurements: TEM imaging to quantify amorphous band formation and distribution at interfaces
In situ or ex situ diffraction analysis to detect loss of crystalline order locally
Stress–strain curves and creep rate measurements from nanoindentation or uniaxial creep tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under sustained loading, there is no significant increase in localized amorphous regions at the multilayer interfaces and the plastic deformation remains dominated solely by conventional dislocation slip (with no evidence of a gradual, gradient-mediated transition), then the hypothesis that strain-induced hyper-range amorphization governs the progressive plastic deformation is falsified.
